newsitem.title: USA: Consumer groups urge Calif Gov. to veto quake plan.
newsitem.headline: Consumer groups urge Calif Gov. to veto quake plan.

text.p: Consumer groups called on California homeowners Thursday to urge Gov. Pete Wilson to veto legislation that would create a $10.5 billion state earthquake insurance agency.

The call was issued by Consumers Union, the nonprofit publisher of Consumer Reports, the Proposition 103 Enforcement Project, a consumer advocacy organization dedicated to insurance reform, and United Policyholders, a group focused on insurance policyholders' rights.
Last week, legislators approved legislation to create the California Earthquake Authority, sending it to the governor.
A spokesman for Wilson said the Republican governor planned to sign the legislation. The signing was expected to take place by the end of the month.

The $10.5 billion authority would be a privately-financed, publicly-managed state agency that would provide insurance coverage for earthquake damage to residential property owners, mobile homeowners and renters in the state.
It would be funded with premiums paid by those who purchase earthquake coverage, cash from participating insurance companies, reinsurance and capital market investors.
But according to the three groups representing the interests of insurance consumers, the authority would be dangerously underfunded.
"The CEA is a house of cards -- it is grossly undercapitalized and likely to collapse after a major quake or series of quakes," said Betsy Imholz, special projects advocate for Consumers Union.
If the CEA runs out of funds, consumers will receive only pro rata claim payments, and may have surcharges added to their policy premiums, Consumers Union said.
"This is a bad deal for consumers and for taxpayers, who will ultimately be asked to make up CEA shortfalls," said Gina Calabrese, senior counsel at the Proposition 103 Enforcement Project.

"It would be unconscionable for the governor to sign into law the CEA bail-out bill, which would transfer the risk of earthquake loss from the state's largest insurers to homeowners and taxpayers," Calabrese said.
